children.text: Collect useful photo and video reviews by requesting a specific product detail, keeping upload optional and preserving the correct product association. Explain the intended use and establish appropriate reuse permission before moving material into other marketing placements. Check private details and the mobile upload path, and keep support attachments separate from public review submissions.
Key takeaways
Ask for useful product context without scripting praise.
A support attachment is not automatically a public review asset.
Check the intended reuse, permission record and final presentation.

A customer photograph can answer a question that a studio image misses: how big the bag looks on a person, how a finish appears in daylight or how a product fits into an ordinary room. The value is in the context. A large folder of unlabelled uploads is much less useful than a few clear examples tied to the correct product.

Build a process for requesting, receiving and using media before asking every buyer for it. The process should explain what would help, give the customer an easy way to participate and make clear how the material may be used.

fields.alt: Judge.me widget settings inside the WhatFlow demo store
fields.caption: Judge.me widget configuration in the WhatFlow demo store. This setup view has no live theme embed enabled; ratings in the widget cards are interface examples.

children.text: Ask for a specific kind of detail

Replace “send us content” with a practical prompt. A homeware store might ask for a photo showing the item in a room. A travel-accessory store might ask what fits inside the organizer. The request helps the customer understand what makes the image useful without scripting a positive review.

Keep the upload optional. A buyer can have a valuable opinion without wanting to photograph their home, family or body. Avoid language suggesting that a text review matters less or that only highly produced videos deserve to be published.
Preserve the product and experience context

Use the review provider’s supported form or collection process so the media remains associated with the correct item. When a customer sends an attachment in a support conversation, do not automatically republish it as a product review. Support evidence and marketing material have different purposes.

WhatFlow can receive WhatsApp media in the inbox, and its Flow integration includes a media-received event. That is useful for handling a conversation. It does not by itself create a public review, a permanent media archive or permission to use the attachment in an advertisement.
Use the same permission checks when
reusing reviews on social media
in another placement.
Make reuse permission explicit

A photo displayed as part of a submitted review is not necessarily cleared for every future campaign. Decide what permissions your intended use requires, explain that use and keep a record of the customer’s agreement where appropriate. Review text and media belong to their authors.

For a paid advertisement, check the proposed crop, caption and placement before publication. Avoid implying that a reviewer endorsed a claim they did not make. A photograph of a product in use does not prove a medical, performance or durability claim on its own.
Keep private details out of the final asset

Inspect backgrounds and metadata-sensitive context before reusing customer material. Address labels, school names, children, personal documents and identifiable interiors may create issues that were not obvious when the image first arrived. Ask for a different image or choose another asset when the context is unsuitable.

Do not solve every problem with a tight crop that changes the meaning of the original photograph. The final presentation should still fairly represent the customer’s experience. Keep the original submission and the approved marketing version distinguishable in your internal process.
Design the upload experience for a phone

Follow your own request from a mobile device. Check how many steps come before the upload, whether the customer can understand file requirements and whether the review is lost if they decide not to attach anything. A clear optional step is often better than a long instruction block.

Judge.me’s current form settings describe which photo and video prompts its product supports. Consult that interface for exact configuration. Your messaging channel can bring the customer to the form, but the form itself has to make the task understandable and manageable.
Include the upload journey in
mobile widget checks
so optional media remains manageable.
Consult
Customizing the review form
for the provider’s supported photo and video prompts.
Publish examples that help a decision

Choose presentation around common buyer questions rather than visual polish alone. A useful image with clear context may explain fit or scale better than a carefully styled but ambiguous shot. Preserve attribution and any relevant disclosure when showing the material elsewhere.

Measure how the content is used and whether it answers recurring questions. Do not attach an invented conversion uplift to a collection of customer photos. The first useful outcome is a more informative product experience supported by material you have the right to display.
Keep the submission and reuse decision together

Hypothetical example: a customer submits a photo showing what fits inside an organizer. The review provider associates it with the product. If the store wants to use that image in a campaign, record the proposed placement, caption, permission status and approved asset separately from the original submission. Check the background for address labels or personal documents before preparing the final version.

A similar image arriving through WhatsApp support may help answer a question without being cleared for publication. WhatFlow Business API can receive that conversation media, but the store still needs the appropriate collection and permission process for public use. Keep a clear decision record so a later colleague can tell why one image is available for the campaign while another remains private support evidence.
Before you put this into practice
Ask for one useful visual detail and allow text-only feedback.
Preserve the product association and original submission context.
Check permission, private details and caption meaning before reuse.

children.text: Respond to a negative product review by acknowledging the specific issue, explaining a factual next step and moving private order details to an appropriate support channel. Apply the same moderation standard to every rating. Resolve the underlying problem on its merits, then let the customer decide whether to update their review without pressure or conditions.
Key takeaways
Acknowledge the actual complaint before explaining policy.
Investigate order details privately through an appropriate channel.
Separate support resolution from requests to change ratings.

A negative review creates two conversations at once. The customer needs a useful response to a specific experience. Future shoppers are watching how the business behaves when something goes wrong. A defensive public reply can make the second conversation worse even if the original problem is fixable.

Start by separating resolution from reputation management. Your job is to understand what happened and explain the next appropriate step. You cannot promise a positive updated review, and resolving the issue should not depend on the customer removing their criticism.

fields.alt: Judge.me widget settings inside the WhatFlow demo store
fields.caption: Judge.me widget configuration in the WhatFlow demo store. This setup view has no live theme embed enabled; ratings in the widget cards are interface examples.

children.text: Read the complaint before choosing a response

Identify whether the review concerns the product, shipping, expectations or the support experience. Check the relevant order privately if you have the necessary information. A complaint about an unclear size guide needs a different response from a parcel that has not arrived.

Avoid beginning with a canned explanation of company policy. Acknowledge the specific issue in plain language: “The strap arriving with a loose stitch is disappointing, and we would like to inspect it with you.” That is more useful than announcing that quality is your highest priority.
Separate
product and service feedback
so the right person investigates the cause.
Keep the public reply concise and factual

A public response should acknowledge the experience, explain an appropriate next step and make the support route clear. Do not publish the buyer’s phone number, address, order details or private correspondence to demonstrate that the business was right. Those details belong in a controlled support conversation.

For example: “We are sorry the replacement part did not fit. Please contact our support team with your order reference so we can check the version and available options.” Only state that you have contacted the customer if the team actually has. Do not imply a resolution that has not happened.
Use a private channel to investigate

The detailed conversation may need photographs, a product identifier or delivery information. Explain why each item is needed, and avoid asking for data the team already has. Record the agreed next step so another colleague can continue the case without making the customer repeat the story.

If WhatsApp is an appropriate, permitted support channel for that customer, WhatFlow’s team inbox can help keep the conversation accessible to the team. It is not permission to contact every reviewer on WhatsApp. Public review data and messaging consent are separate parts of the customer relationship.
Use
Publishing and hiding reviews
to understand the provider’s review statuses before applying your store’s moderation decision.
Follow the same moderation standard for every rating

Spam, private information and irrelevant content can need moderation. A low rating alone should not become the reason honest feedback disappears. Write a moderation policy that a colleague can apply consistently, then use your review provider’s supported statuses and reporting tools.

Judge.me documents separate published, pending, hidden and archived review states. The exact behavior of those states belongs to its current product documentation. Do not assume hiding a storefront review removes it from every other feed or channel where it might have been shared.
Apply
consistent review moderation
when content needs review beyond its rating.
Turn repeated complaints into product work

Review cases together rather than treating every critical message as an isolated exception. Repeated fit complaints may indicate an unclear product description. Repeated missing-accessory reports may point to packaging. A long response delay may mean the inbox needs a clearer owner during busy hours.

Keep a short issue log with the theme, affected product, frequency and proposed change. Avoid copying unnecessary personal details into that log. Assign a person and a review date to the improvement; otherwise the same complaint will keep receiving polished replies without a better customer experience.
Close the support loop without bargaining over the review

Tell the customer what was done and what remains open. If they choose to update the review, that decision is theirs. Do not make a replacement or other appropriate support outcome conditional on a new rating. The resolution and the public feedback should remain honest.

A careful reply does not guarantee that every reader will buy. It does show that the store can acknowledge a problem and follow through. Over time, that operational consistency is more credible than a page that appears to have never disappointed anyone.
Use a reply-to-resolution case note

Imagine a customer saying a replacement lid still leaks. A useful public reply can acknowledge that the replacement has not solved the problem and offer a clear support route. It should not publish the order history to prove how much work the team has done. Privately, ask for the lid version or evidence needed to investigate, using information already held wherever possible. Avoid repeating the same request at each handoff.

Keep a short controlled note covering the reported problem, what has been checked, the next decision owner and when the customer will hear back. If the issue reveals a recurring compatibility error, assign a separate product-page or fulfillment fix. When the case closes, record the actual resolution rather than “review recovered.” WhatFlow can help colleagues continue an appropriate WhatsApp conversation, but the public review remains the customer’s account of the experience and the provider controls its editing process.
Before you put this into practice
Write a specific public acknowledgment.
Name the next decision and its owner.
Check repeated complaints for a product or process fix.

children.text: A useful review request identifies the store and product, asks for honest experience and provides the correct review link. Keep reminders optional in tone and suppress completed reviewers where supported. WhatsApp examples are drafts, not approved templates; check the applicable message format and permissions, and make sure someone monitors any support replies the invitation encourages.
Key takeaways
Identify the purchase and make the review destination clear.
Ask for honest detail without steering the rating.
Test message variables and support replies before sending.

A review request does not need to sound like a campaign announcement. The customer needs to recognize the purchase, understand what you are asking and find the right link. Anything that obscures those three things adds effort to a task they are doing for your business.

The examples below are writing starting points. They are not pre-approved WhatsApp templates, actual customer messages or promises of a particular response rate. Adapt them to your product, permissions and review provider before using them in a live sequence.

fields.alt: Judge.me widget settings inside the WhatFlow demo store
fields.caption: Judge.me widget configuration in the WhatFlow demo store. This setup view has no live theme embed enabled; ratings in the widget cards are interface examples.

children.text: Start with the product, not the brand’s ambition

A vague message asking the buyer to “support our journey” makes the request about the store. A more useful invitation identifies the item and asks about the customer’s experience. Mentioning the product also helps someone who has placed several recent orders find the correct context.

A simple email opening could be: “How is the insulated lunch bag working for you? We would appreciate an honest review of what you liked and what could be better.” Follow it with a clearly labeled review link. Avoid adding several promotional buttons around the main task.
Choose
review invitation timing
that gives buyers a reasonable opportunity to use the product.
A short WhatsApp invitation

A concise draft is: “Hi [first name], this is [store]. When you have had a chance to use [product], you can share an honest review here: [review link]. If you need help with the order, reply to this message.” Each placeholder needs a real, appropriate value before sending.

Do not assume a short message is unrestricted. Eligible outbound WhatsApp messages may require an approved template, and the customer must meet the applicable messaging requirements. A conversational tone is a writing choice; it does not replace the channel’s rules or a working opt-out process.
A reminder that adds clarity rather than pressure

A reminder can acknowledge that the buyer may not have had time: “A quick follow-up about [product]: if you would like to share your experience, your review link is [link]. There is no need to reply if you have already reviewed it.” Use reliable suppression where the tools support it.

If you cannot identify completed reviewers across channels, say less and send fewer reminders. Repeatedly asking someone who already submitted feedback undermines the care the first message tried to convey. Decide which system owns the reminder schedule instead of letting every installed app run independently.
Use the
WhatsApp Business messaging policy
to check applicable messaging permission and channel requirements; a relevant message still needs the appropriate sending process.
Ask for useful detail without steering the rating

A product-specific prompt can help: “What was the fit like, and how did the fabric feel after washing?” That invites information a future buyer can use. It is different from telling the customer that a five-star rating would help the store or implying that criticism is unwelcome.

For photo requests, explain what would be useful and make the addition optional. “A photo showing the bag in everyday use is welcome” is more concrete than “send amazing content.” Obtain the appropriate permission before reusing the image in advertising or other marketing placements.
Give support replies a real destination

If the invitation says “reply if you need help,” someone needs to read those replies. Decide who checks the inbox, how order context is found and when a question should move to another colleague. The request is part of a customer relationship, not just a link-delivery exercise.

WhatFlow’s shared inbox can support that conversational handoff without inbox seat fees on Business API plans. Review storage, publication and verification remain the review provider’s responsibility. Avoid telling customers that a WhatsApp reply itself will appear as a product review unless your actual integration does that.
Define
support conversation ownership
before inviting customers to reply with a problem.
Edit against the phone screen

Read the finished message on a small screen. Remove an introductory sentence if it delays recognition of the product. Check that the link opens the intended form, that the language matches the customer and that the sender identity is clear. Test placeholders with missing values before automating them.

The final check is simple: would the customer understand the request without knowing your internal marketing goal? If they can recognize the purchase, leave an honest answer and ask for help, the message has done its job.
Adapt the same request to a real product question

For a hypothetical insulated lunch bag, an email could ask: “How has the lunch bag worked for your usual container? Share what fits well and what could be better: [review link].” A WhatsApp draft could say: “Hi [name], this is [store]. If you have tried [product], we welcome your honest review: [link]. Reply here if you need order help.” These are writing examples; replace placeholders and check the actual approved WhatsApp setup before use.

Use the invitation to ask about experience rather than to solicit a particular rating. Test a missing first name, a long product title and an order containing several products. Decide whether the destination makes the product choice clear instead of adding every item to a crowded message. For the reminder, verify the completed-review exclusion across the tools you use. If that connection is absent, keep the follow-up modest and explain the limitation internally.
Before you put this into practice
Replace and validate every placeholder.
Check the form on a phone without staff access.
Confirm who reads replies and handles opt-outs.

children.text: Send a product review request after the customer has a reasonable opportunity to receive and use the item. Start from reliable delivery information where available, then choose a delay suited to the product’s learning or usage cycle. Compare similar orders and monitor premature-request replies; there is no single delay that fits every Shopify catalog.
Key takeaways
Fulfillment and delivery are different scheduling events.
Group products by how long a meaningful experience takes.
Treat “not used it yet” replies as timing feedback.

“Send the request three days later” sounds like a complete strategy until you sell two very different products. A buyer can comment on a tote bag almost immediately. A garden kit may need assembly, weather and a weekend before the customer knows whether it was useful. Timing should reflect that experience.

The right question is when a buyer has enough information to give a helpful answer. Your first schedule is a hypothesis. Build it from the delivery experience and expected product use, then revise it using customer responses rather than a borrowed universal conversion figure.

fields.alt: Judge.me widget settings inside the WhatFlow demo store
fields.caption: Judge.me widget configuration in the WhatFlow demo store. This setup view has no live theme embed enabled; ratings in the widget cards are interface examples.

children.text: Separate order date, fulfillment and delivery

An order date tells you when the purchase was recorded. Fulfillment tells you about the store’s shipping process. Delivery, when available and reliable, is closer to the buyer actually having the product. Those timestamps serve different purposes and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Write down which event your current reminder uses. If a workflow starts from fulfillment but the message says “now that your order has arrived,” the wording may get ahead of reality. Fix that mismatch before testing a new delay or a more enthusiastic subject line.
Consult
How Judge.me collects reviews
to distinguish collection routes before attributing their results to timing.
Group products by how they are experienced

Create a few practical groups rather than a custom schedule for every SKU. An immediately usable accessory, a product requiring setup and a consumable that needs repeated use can each have a different starting delay. Keep the grouping simple enough that the team can maintain it.

Gift purchases deserve additional thought. The purchaser may not be the person using the item, and an early request can arrive before the occasion. Offer a polite invitation that allows the customer to answer later rather than assuming every buyer has already tested the product personally.
Build the schedule into a
first product review process
that includes the form and support path.
Make exceptions part of the schedule

A return, replacement or open delivery problem can make a routine request feel careless. Where supported data is available, define how your process handles those situations. Do not promise that an app will suppress every exception unless the conditions are actually configured and tested.

The customer must still be able to leave honest feedback. Handling an unresolved support issue is different from selectively asking only satisfied buyers to post publicly. Keep your collection policy neutral and provide an accessible review route regardless of whether the experience was positive.
Test a single timing change

Choose comparable orders and change one delay at a time. Record how many orders were eligible, how many invitations reached the intended recipients and how many useful reviews followed. Also record replies saying that the parcel has not arrived or that the buyer has not used the item yet.

Those replies can be more informative than a small movement in submission rate. They tell you whether the schedule fits the real customer journey. Avoid declaring a winner after only a few orders, especially when one group contains products with a different price or delivery method.
Use consistent denominators from
review collection measurement
when comparing timing tests.
Coordinate the channels before adding reminders

If your review app sends email and another workflow sends WhatsApp, decide whether they form one planned sequence or duplicate each other. The buyer experiences the combined contact volume. Different dashboards do not make repeated requests feel like different conversations.

WhatFlow can provide the WhatsApp conversation and inbox side of the process. Use an eligible approved template when the invitation is outside the active customer-service window, and respect the customer’s messaging preferences. The review app controls its form, scheduling capabilities and verification rules.
Review the schedule as the business changes

Revisit timing when shipping routes, product categories or customer expectations change. A schedule that worked for locally stocked items can become unsuitable after adding preorders. Keep a short note explaining the chosen event and delay so a new colleague can understand the reasoning.

Start with a schedule that feels reasonable from the customer’s side, measure the whole sequence and improve the part that causes confusion. More requests are useful only when the recipient has something meaningful to say and an easy way to say it.
Create a product-use timing table

Hypothetical example: group a catalog into a ready-to-use tote and a self-assembly shelf. Begin a timing test from a supported delivery signal and allow the shelf more time because assembly must happen first. Record the chosen delay, the reason for it and how the workflow handles a missing delivery event. These are test choices, not recommended universal waiting periods.

When reviewing results, separate product groups and keep the reporting window consistent. Count eligible orders, invitations, submissions and replies saying the request arrived too soon. If the shelf group needs more time, adjust that group rather than delaying every request. Keep email and WhatsApp invitations on the same schedule so a timing experiment does not accidentally become a frequency experiment.
Before you put this into practice
Name the actual event starting the timer.
Document the usage reason for each product group’s delay.
Review early-request replies before adding reminders.

children.text: Collect your first Shopify product reviews by inviting real buyers after they have had time to use the item, linking directly to the correct review form and asking for honest feedback. Give support replies an owner and check product associations. Track eligible orders, invitations and submissions separately so early problems can be fixed before increasing request volume.
Key takeaways
Invite real buyers without scripting a positive verdict.
Make the correct product review form easy to reach.
Trace the whole process before adding more reminders.

A new product page has an awkward problem: shoppers want reassurance, but the customers who could provide it have only just started buying. The answer is not to fill the gap with invented testimonials. It is to build a repeatable way for real buyers to describe what happened after the order arrived.

For a small store, a good review process can fit on one page. Decide who should receive a request, when they will have something useful to say, where they should leave it and who will handle replies. Start there before adding coupons, several reminders or another automation app.

fields.alt: Judge.me widget settings inside the WhatFlow demo store
fields.caption: Judge.me widget configuration in the WhatFlow demo store. This setup view has no live theme embed enabled; ratings in the widget cards are interface examples.

children.text: Give the customer time to experience the product

An order confirmation is usually too early to ask how the product performed. Delivery may be a better starting point, followed by a delay that reflects actual use. A mug can be assessed quickly; a product requiring installation or several uses needs a different schedule. These are decisions for your store, not universal timing rules.

If you cannot reliably identify delivery, describe the request carefully and avoid claiming that you know the parcel arrived. Let the buyer tell you if it has not. That response is an operational issue worth resolving before you continue a routine reminder sequence.
Choose
review request timing
around a meaningful product experience.
Ask one clear question and provide one destination

A practical request explains which product you mean and gives the buyer a direct route to the appropriate review form. Ask for an honest account, including what worked and what could be improved. A customer should not have to navigate several product pages to find the correct place to write.

For example: “How did the ceramic travel mug work for you? Share your experience here when you have a moment.” Treat this as draft wording, not an approved WhatsApp template. The actual message must use the right channel permissions and any required template approval.
Keep reviews and support connected

Some customers answer the request with a question about a missing part, a return or a delayed shipment. Give those messages an owner. A review invitation should not become a dead end because the merchant expected a form submission rather than a conversation.

WhatFlow Business API can help a Shopify team handle WhatsApp conversations in its shared inbox. Review collection and verification still belong to your review provider. Sending a customer a form link through WhatsApp does not automatically make the eventual review a verified purchase review.
Use
Judge.me verified-review requirements
when explaining what the provider can label as verified.
Measure the process from eligible order to published review

Track a small set of counts: eligible orders, requests actually sent, submissions received and published reviews. Use consistent definitions and a fixed reporting period. If ten requests produce two submissions, that is a small sample to learn from, not a benchmark for every future product.

Look for the first point where the process breaks. Missing phone numbers suggest a contact-data issue. Requests sent before arrival suggest a timing problem. Form visits without submissions may point to a long or confusing form. A bigger reminder schedule will not fix all three.
Use the right
review funnel denominators
to identify where the process breaks.
Build a routine before increasing volume

Review a handful of completed customer journeys each week. Open the message, follow its link on a phone and check the resulting review’s product association. Make sure the public page displays the feedback correctly and that private contact details have not been exposed.

As volume grows, automate the stable parts and keep exceptions visible. WhatFlow includes features across Business API plans and does not charge inbox seat fees, which can make it easier to involve another colleague. Message allowances, rates and the review app’s own terms still determine the total cost.
A useful first-month outcome

Success in the first month is a working process you can explain and repeat: real customers receive a relevant invitation, their answers reach the right place and someone responds when help is needed. A smaller set of credible reviews is a stronger foundation than a page crowded with unsupported claims.
Diagnose a first batch of invitations

Hypothetical example: 20 orders qualify for a first invitation batch, 16 invitations are sent, and three submissions reach the provider. The missing four sends and the gap between invitations and submissions are separate questions. Check contact eligibility and event mapping first, then follow the form on a phone. These example counts describe a diagnostic exercise, not a review-rate benchmark.

Inspect each submission’s product, date and source label before checking its storefront display. Ask a colleague to reply to one controlled invitation as though a part were missing; the conversation should reach a monitored route. WhatFlow Business API can support that WhatsApp conversation while the review provider retains responsibility for the form, publication and verification. Fix the earliest broken stage before increasing audience size.
Before you put this into practice
Follow one invitation link on a phone.
Confirm the submitted review belongs to the intended product.
Give customer questions from invitations a named owner.

children.text: Use Shopify Sidekick on desktop to draft an inactive Flow workflow from a precise event, condition and intended action. Then inspect the actual WhatFlow Business API tasks, recipient variables and order references in Flow. Keep the draft inactive while checking positive, nonmatching and repeated-event cases; the generated diagram and configuration screenshots do not establish message delivery.
Key takeaways
Describe the intended business rule and explicitly request an inactive draft.
Select a missing WhatFlow task manually rather than accepting a substitute.
Review generated fields and branches separately from any later delivery check.
Describe the store outcome before describing the technology

You do not need to start an automation project with an API specification. A merchant can start with a plain sentence: when a customer confirms the order in WhatsApp, record that confirmation on the correct Shopify order. The event, rule and outcome are already present in that sentence.

Shopify supports generating Flow workflows with Sidekick from a plain-language description on desktop. WhatFlow Business API supplies WhatsApp triggers and actions that you can select in Flow. Together, they offer an approachable way to move from an idea to a visual workflow, with a review step before anything goes live.
What Sidekick does, and what you should check yourself

Sidekick can generate workflow elements for review and modification. Shopify documents that generated workflows start inactive and can omit business-specific logic in complex requests. Treat the result as a first draft: inspect the selected trigger, each condition and the fields passed into the action.

An AI-generated description is not proof that the correct WhatFlow task was selected. If Sidekick does not add the installed WhatFlow trigger or action you need, choose it manually in Flow. Standard field mapping does not require writing API code, but it still requires understanding which customer or order the event refers to.
Shopify’s
Generate a workflow with Sidekick
documents generation, inactive drafts and the review process.

fields.alt: Shopify Sidekick assisting with a plain-language request for an inactive WhatFlow workflow
fields.caption: Sidekick-assisted demo workflow. AI-generated steps need review; the demonstration is kept inactive and does not send customer messages.

children.text: What Sidekick built in the demo store

We asked Sidekick to create an inactive delivery-information workflow using WhatsApp Text Message Received, an exact DELIVERY_INFO condition and Send WhatsApp Text Message addressed to fromPhoneNumber. Its preview contained all three steps. We added the draft to the store, inspected the action’s recipient and sample message, and left it inactive.

That is the workflow shown beside the Sidekick conversation in the screenshot. It demonstrates generation and configuration, not delivery. The order-tagging prompt below is a separate exercise, shown in its own manually configured demo screenshot. Always inspect the actual fields rather than relying only on Sidekick’s prose summary.
Step 1: open Flow and write a precise request

On desktop, open Shopify Flow and then Sidekick. Include the event, condition, intended action and a clear instruction to keep the result inactive. For an order-reply exercise, a useful request is: “Draft an inactive workflow using WhatFlow WhatsApp Order Reply. When Reply Type is BUTTON and Button Text matches my configured confirmation label, add WF_COD_CONFIRMED to the order supplied by the trigger. Leave other replies for manual review. Do not send messages or activate the workflow.”

Replace the confirmation label with the one your message actually uses. If you have not defined that label yet, keep the workflow as an unfinished draft rather than treating placeholder text as a working condition.
Step 2: inspect the event and the available order reference

Open the generated workflow and check that its trigger is WhatsApp Order Reply. The generic WhatsApp Button Clicked event is useful for intent routing, but it should not be substituted for an order-aware event merely because both involve a button.

Inspect which order the action uses. The trigger’s supplied order reference is different from a fixed order selected during a demo. A production workflow must resolve the intended order for each event. Include a controlled test where the same buyer has more than one order.
For the order-aware exercise, follow the
order-reply configuration
rather than substituting a generic button event.

fields.alt: Inactive Shopify Flow example branching on a WhatsApp order reply and adding an order tag
fields.caption: Inactive demo workflow: a WhatsApp order reply is checked before an order tag is added. The screenshot does not show a live order being changed or fulfilled.

children.text: Step 3: review the true and false branches

The positive branch should represent the exact business decision in the request. A matching confirmation can add the intended tag. A question, negative response or nonmatching button should not silently pass through the same positive branch.

Check existing tags or another appropriate guard if the same reply can arrive more than once. Do not let the AI broaden a simple tagging exercise into cancellation, refund or fulfillment actions. Those outcomes need their own explicit store rules.
A second prompt: draft an outbound message workflow

For an outbound exercise, describe a supported Shopify event and the template outcome: “Draft an inactive workflow for an appropriate fulfillment event. Check that the required customer phone and tracking values exist, then add WhatFlow Send WhatsApp Template. Leave the exact approved template name and variables for me to review. Do not activate or send a test message.”

The request deliberately does not invent an approved template name or assume an order-created event contains tracking data. After generation, select the actual approved template and map the fields from the event. If Sidekick cannot add the WhatFlow action, insert it through Flow’s action picker.
Use the separate
template field mapping
walkthrough when reviewing an outbound draft.

fields.alt: WhatFlow Send WhatsApp Template configuration in Shopify Flow with template and recipient fields
fields.caption: WhatFlow template action in the demo Flow editor. Template names and variable choices must match the approved template in your own account.

children.text: Review recipient, timing and message rules

Before activation, check that the recipient is a supplied customer variable rather than a demonstration number. Review every template placeholder, the intended language and any media or button input. Confirm what happens when required data is missing.

The message format must still meet WhatsApp requirements. Free-form text, interactive buttons, CTA links and separate media actions require an active customer-service window; eligible messages outside it use approved templates. Sidekick cannot remove those channel rules.
Test the business rule, not just the generated diagram

Use controlled recipients and test orders. Check a positive case, a nonmatching response, missing data and duplicate events. Inspect the resulting Shopify state and the WhatFlow conversation. A generated workflow that looks plausible is not the same as a tested workflow.

Keep the draft inactive until the logic and final outcome match the request. Shopify lets merchants continue refining the workflow manually or with Sidekick. Apply a change only after checking what it modifies, especially when a new branch adds an external action.
Keep the finished workflow understandable to your team

Give the workflow a descriptive name and add a note explaining its purpose, required template and exception path. The next colleague should be able to see why a branch exists without reading the original AI conversation. That is where visual automation is most useful for a nontechnical team.

WhatFlow Business API includes its features across plans, including Free, with no inbox seat fees. The team can start with a small workflow and involve more colleagues in the conversation without a separate seat subscription. Message allowances, rates and the terms of Shopify or other apps still apply.
Keep a prompt-to-configuration review note

Beside the inactive draft, record three lines: requested rule, actual selected steps and remaining gaps. For the supplied DELIVERY_INFO demo, inspect the exact text condition and fromPhoneNumber recipient. Keep the separate order-tagging exercise in its own note so a colleague does not mistake the demonstrated text workflow for a completed order-confirmation process.
Before you put this into practice
Keep the generated workflow inactive during review.
Confirm the installed trigger and recipient variable in the editor.
Check false, repeated-event and missing-data cases.
Record which checks inspect logic and which would require a separate controlled end-to-end exercise.

children.text: Connect WhatFlow Business API to another Shopify app through Flow when the installed apps expose compatible triggers and actions and supply the identifiers each step needs. Verify the connector setup, any separate plan requirement and the recipient mapping. Treat the guide’s app combinations as blueprints; the inactive screenshots do not prove that every third-party route has executed.
Key takeaways
An app listing or integration logo does not expose every feature as a Flow task.
A customer ID needs a supported recipient lookup before a WhatsApp send.
Third-party app plans remain separate from WhatFlow’s all-feature plans.
Your store already has useful automation building blocks

A review app knows when it wants to request feedback. Shopify knows when an order reaches a particular stage. A WhatsApp customer can tell you they need help by replying to a message. Flow is useful because it can connect compatible events and actions without asking the merchant to build a separate integration server.

WhatFlow Business API contributes incoming WhatsApp triggers and outgoing message actions to that environment. The benefit is practical: a merchant can often compose a workflow from installed steps in Shopify’s editor, keep the business rule visible and adjust it as the store changes.
Review the
WhatFlow Flow foundations
before combining installed app tasks.

fields.alt: Shopify Add order tags action mapped to the order supplied by a WhatFlow reply workflow
fields.caption: Inactive demo: Shopify’s Add order tags action uses order.id from the WhatFlow order-reply event. Other app blueprints require their own compatible connectors and setup.

children.text: Check three things before combining apps

First, both sides need the relevant Flow capability. An app appearing in the Shopify App Store does not mean every feature is available as a Flow task. Second, install and configure the connector or connection required for that task. Third, confirm that the trigger supplies the identifiers and fields the next action needs.

For example, a WhatsApp sender number is not automatically a helpdesk customer ID, and a generic button event is not automatically an order. If the next step needs a missing value, the workflow needs a supported lookup, a different trigger or a human step. The visual editor makes the connection easier to build; it cannot invent missing business data.
Check
Shopify Flow connectors
for installation and connection requirements alongside the actual app tasks.
Blueprint 1: a Judge.me review request becomes a WhatsApp message

WhatFlow includes a Flow template named Send WhatsApp review request for Judge.me reviews. Its purpose is to send a WhatsApp review request when Judge.me emits the relevant review-request event. Use the installed template and inspect the actual trigger fields in your store before adapting it.

The recipe is straightforward: the review-request event starts the flow, conditions check the required customer details and messaging permission, and WhatFlow sends an eligible approved template containing the correct review link. The template must match the variables used by the action. A review request sent after the customer-service window should not be replaced with an unrestricted free-form message.

Test the destination link and recipient using controlled data. If you also run another review-reminder sequence, decide which app owns the reminder schedule so the customer does not receive overlapping requests. The screenshot illustrates the Flow composition model; it is not a claim that every third-party blueprint has been run in this demo store.
Two details from the live Judge.me connector

In the demo store’s installed connector, Review request ready explicitly requires Judge.me’s paid Awesome plan and the Send Verified Trigger setting in Integrations. WhatFlow’s all-feature plans do not remove that separate Judge.me requirement. Check your installed connector before budgeting or following the recipe.

The trigger’s variables include customer_id, order_id, buyer_first_name, product_title, product_image_url and product_review_url, but the variable list we inspected did not include a buyer phone number. A customer ID is not a recipient phone number. Use a supported lookup that resolves the intended customer and permitted WhatsApp number before sending, or leave the workflow inactive until that mapping is available. Our template-action screenshot uses a Shopify order event with order.phone; it does not demonstrate a completed Judge.me-to-WhatsApp send.

fields.alt: WhatFlow Send WhatsApp Template configuration in Shopify Flow with template and recipient fields
fields.caption: WhatFlow template action in the demo Flow editor. Template names and variable choices must match the approved template in your own account.

children.text: Blueprint 2: an order reply changes the store’s next step

Choose WhatsApp Order Reply when the customer’s response needs to affect an identified Shopify order. Check the actual reply type and button value, then use a supported order-tag action to record the result. A clearly named tag can help a fulfillment team distinguish confirmed orders from those awaiting attention.

A different branch can represent a request for help. If a compatible installed helpdesk exposes a suitable action, use that action with the required identifiers and a concise description of the issue. Do not claim that a ticket exists until the action is configured and its run result confirms it. Without that connector, keep the handoff in the WhatFlow team inbox.
Use the
order-aware reply recipe
when the next action needs a specific order.

fields.alt: Inactive Shopify Flow example branching on a WhatsApp order reply and adding an order tag
fields.caption: Inactive demo workflow: a WhatsApp order reply is checked before an order tag is added. The screenshot does not show a live order being changed or fulfilled.

children.text: Blueprint 3: record an operational event for the team

Some stores use a connected spreadsheet or internal notification action for a lightweight operations log. A WhatFlow event can contribute a timestamp and a short status when the installed connector supports the required action and authentication. Use only the fields the team actually needs.

A spreadsheet should not become a copy of every private conversation. Avoid logging full message bodies, customer attachment links or unnecessary phone numbers by default. Received media download URLs can expire and should not be treated as permanent file storage. The logging action should help the operational process rather than create a second uncontrolled inbox.
Blueprint 4: an app milestone starts a relevant customer message

A compatible loyalty, subscription or customer-segmentation app may expose a useful milestone through Flow. When it does, a store can evaluate the event and send an appropriate WhatFlow template, provided the trigger supplies the recipient data and the store has the required permission.

Keep the message tied to the actual milestone and check duplicate behavior. A customer becoming eligible for a tier, a subscription renewing and a payment failing deserve different wording and rules. Validate the exact app task in your installed version rather than assuming every loyalty or subscription app uses the same trigger name.
Keep one owner for each customer-facing automation

It is easy for several apps to react to the same order event. Before activating a new workflow, list the messages already sent by Shopify, WhatFlow and your other apps. Decide which system owns each notification and how the others should behave.

Then test the whole path: event, condition, recipient, message, external action and human handoff. A diagram with several app logos can look complete while one required field is missing. The actual run history and the final customer experience are the useful checks.
Why WhatFlow fits this style of Shopify automation

The tight Shopify integration means the merchant can work with familiar events, order data and visual steps rather than maintaining an independent automation stack for every task. WhatFlow’s inbox gives the team a place to continue the conversation when a branch needs a person.

WhatFlow Business API includes its features across plans and does not charge per inbox seat. Message allowances and rates determine the plan, while Shopify and third-party apps keep their own pricing. That combination is especially useful when a small team wants several people involved in the workflow without multiplying support-seat costs.
Record the missing field before extending a blueprint

For the documented Judge.me blueprint, write down the paid-plan and Send Verified Trigger requirements beside the installed event. Then record that its inspected variables omit a buyer phone number. Leave the draft inactive until a supported lookup supplies the intended permitted recipient; the order.phone mapping in a different screenshot is not a completed solution to that gap.

Confirm the exact installed trigger and action.
Verify third-party plan and connection requirements.
Map every required identifier and recipient field.
Assign one owner to the reminder schedule and exception path.

children.text: To configure a WhatsApp template in Shopify Flow, choose an event supplying the required data, add WhatFlow Business API’s Send WhatsApp Template action and map the intended recipient. Use the exact approved template name, language and matching variables. Review missing values and repeated events while inactive; an accepted Flow step is not proof of delivery or reading.
Key takeaways
Choose the event around what the message can truthfully establish.
Map only the variables required by the actual approved template.
Keep request acceptance, delivery and reading as separate outcomes.
A message should follow the event the customer cares about

An order being created, a fulfillment being recorded and a parcel being delivered are different events. Start a messaging workflow from the event that actually supports the statement in your message. If the template promises tracking details, an order-created event may be too early to supply them.

WhatFlow Business API adds Send WhatsApp Template to Shopify Flow, alongside text, interactive and media actions. The configuration happens in Shopify’s visual editor. You still need to choose an appropriate event, an approved template and the correct customer data; visual configuration does not remove those decisions.
Step 1: prepare the template before building the workflow

Create the intended message in WhatFlow’s template tools and wait for the required approval. Check the exact template name, language, header type, body variables and any URL-button variable. A variable slot expecting an order reference should not receive a phone number simply because both values are available in Flow.

Keep the wording accurate for the event. A fulfillment notification can explain that an order has been fulfilled when the store’s fulfillment event supports that statement. It should not claim that the carrier delivered the parcel unless the trigger and data establish delivery.
Use the
message action overview
to choose between templates and active-window formats.
Step 2: choose a trigger with the data your message requires

In an inactive Flow workflow, choose a supported Shopify or installed-app trigger that supplies the relevant order, customer and event data. Inspect its available variables before adding conditions. For a fulfillment-oriented notification, use an appropriate fulfillment event and check that the required tracking values exist when it runs.

An order can have several fulfillments. Decide whether you want a message per fulfillment or a message only after a defined overall state. That business rule belongs in the workflow; otherwise a split shipment can produce more messages than your customer expects.

fields.alt: WhatFlow Send WhatsApp Template configuration in Shopify Flow with template and recipient fields
fields.caption: WhatFlow template action in the demo Flow editor. Template names and variable choices must match the approved template in your own account.

children.text: The configuration shown in our screenshots

The demo uses Shopify’s Order created trigger with the approved utility template wf_order_confirm_req_v1. The recipient is order.phone, and Shopify supplies order.id and order.customer.id as context. The template was checked in the demo app’s template preview; its six body placeholders represent the name, order number, subtotal, total, address and city.

We mapped those placeholders to the shipping first name, order name, presentment-currency subtotal and total amounts, shipping address line and city. The following screenshot shows the body inputs. Add the required currency formatting, missing-phone and missing-address checks, and messaging-permission rules for your own store. This is an inactive field-mapping demonstration, not a complete production notification policy. No message was sent, and existing WhatFlow order notifications should be checked for overlap before you enable an equivalent Flow.

fields.alt: WhatFlow template body variables mapped to Shopify order number, subtotal, total, address and city
fields.caption: Body variables in the inactive order-confirmation demo. These are field mappings, not customer data or proof of sending. Review currency formatting, missing values and permissions before activation.

children.text: Step 3: add Send WhatsApp Template and map the recipient

Select WhatFlow and Send WhatsApp Template. Use the exact approved template name. Choose a recipient variable that actually contains the intended customer’s phone number, and apply an appropriate condition when the number or required permission is absent. A test number typed into the editor must not remain as the recipient of every production event.

WhatFlow accepts an international-format number or a local number with the corresponding country code where the action supports it. Do not guess the country from a name or language. Use the data available to your store and confirm the resulting number with a controlled test.
Step 4: match each variable to the approved message

The template action exposes header inputs where relevant, body parameters, a URL-button variable and optional order and customer references. Map the supplied fields to the actual approved structure rather than filling every available input. A template with two body placeholders does not need seven unrelated values.

Retain order and customer references when the event and action support them. Those references help an order-aware conversation carry useful context for later handling. Test replies as well as the outbound message, especially when a buyer can have more than one active order.
Retain supported order context for later
order-aware reply handling
when a customer answers.

fields.alt: Shopify Flow action picker listing WhatFlow WhatsApp message actions
fields.caption: WhatFlow message actions available in the demo store’s Shopify Flow editor. Message type and customer-service-window rules still apply.

children.text: When to choose the other seven actions

An incoming conversation may be better served by a short text, up to three interactive buttons, a CTA link, or an image, video, audio or document message. These are separate WhatFlow actions. Choose the message format that helps the buyer complete the next step, rather than sending a large block of text for every situation.

Free-form text, interactive, CTA and separate media messages require an active customer-service window. Outside that window, use an eligible approved template. Media actions need a supported, accessible direct media URL; a received Meta media ID is not interchangeable with that URL.
A successful Flow step is not a delivery receipt

Review both the Flow run and the WhatFlow conversation when testing. A message accepted for sending is not the same as a message delivered to the recipient, and delivery is not the same as a read receipt. Do not interpret a green workflow result as proof that the customer saw the message.

Check missing variables, absent phone numbers, an unapproved template and duplicate events as part of your test plan. If a message needs review after an uncertain send outcome, avoid blindly triggering another copy. Make the staff recovery process explicit before activating a high-volume event.
Shopify’s
Testing workflows in Shopify Flow
explains why a logic preview cannot establish an actual customer send.
Understand the cost of the whole workflow

WhatFlow Business API provides feature access across plans, including Free, and has no inbox seat fees. Plans differ by message allowances and rates. That lets a store start with one valuable notification without buying a higher feature tier just to access the workflow tools.

WhatsApp’s applicable messaging charges and Shopify or connected-app costs still matter. A narrow transactional notification is usually easier to budget and evaluate than an assortment of loosely defined messages. Start with a controlled test, inspect the actual outcome and expand from there.
Compare the approved preview with each mapped input

For the inactive six-placeholder order-confirmation demo, keep the approved preview beside the Flow editor and label each input by its meaning: name, order number, subtotal, total, address and city. Check currency formatting and missing-value handling at the same time. The sample template name belongs to the documented demo; use the approved structure from your own account.
Before you put this into practice
Confirm the actual template approval, name and language.
Choose a recipient field and handle missing phone data.
Match every input to its placeholder and formatting needs.
Check duplicate notifications and split-fulfillment behavior.
Keep the sample inactive until configuration review is complete.

children.text: Route incoming WhatsApp messages in Shopify Flow by selecting WhatFlow Business API’s text-message trigger, checking a narrow condition and mapping the reply recipient from the incoming sender field. Keep order changes on an order-aware path. Review nonmatching text, repeated messages and human handoffs while inactive, and use free-form replies only within the applicable customer-service window.
Key takeaways
An incoming sender number is not a resolved Shopify order.
Start with a narrow request condition before broadening intent matching.
An invitation to reply TEAM does not itself assign a colleague.
Start with the questions your team answers every day

“How long does delivery take?” is a good candidate for a short automated answer. “My parcel arrived damaged and I need help” needs a different path. A useful support workflow recognizes a narrow request, gives the customer an appropriate next step and leaves room for the team to take over.

WhatFlow Business API brings incoming WhatsApp events into Shopify Flow. You can build the basic rule in the visual editor without creating a webhook or writing API code. This guide describes a first-response recipe; it does not assume that every incoming phone number has already been matched to a Shopify customer or order.
Step 1: select WhatsApp Text Message Received

Open Flow, create an inactive workflow and choose WhatFlow’s WhatsApp Text Message Received trigger. Inspect the supplied fields, especially Message Body, Sender Phone Number and Profile Name. Use the message body to evaluate the request and the sender number to address a response.

The profile name is useful conversation context, but it is not an authenticated Shopify customer identity. Similarly, the sender number alone should not be used to decide which of several orders to change. Use the order-specific reply trigger when your next action requires an order reference.
Choose the
order-specific reply trigger
when a branch needs an identified order.

fields.alt: Inactive Shopify Flow example using an incoming WhatsApp message and a condition to choose a reply
fields.caption: Inactive demo workflow: an incoming WhatsApp text message is evaluated before a response action. Review the condition and recipient mapping before enabling your own version.

children.text: Step 2: keep the first condition narrow

For a controlled example, use a dedicated test keyword such as DELIVERY_INFO rather than a broad rule that treats every mention of delivery as the same question. That makes the first test predictable. Once the basic mapping works, decide which real phrases your store should recognize and which should go to a person.

A complaint mentioning delivery is not necessarily a request for the delivery policy. Check how the condition behaves with questions, negation, mixed languages and unrelated text. Avoid sending several overlapping automated responses when one message matches more than one workflow.
Step 3: choose a concise reply or a small set of choices

Add Send WhatsApp Text Message for a short answer, or Send WhatsApp Interactive Buttons when the next step benefits from choices. The button action supports up to three quick replies. For example, a support greeting could offer Delivery, Returns and Speak to team, using the actual labels configured in your action.

Map the recipient from the incoming sender-number field. These free-form actions require an active WhatsApp customer-service window. An incoming message normally creates that context, but a long delay can change the situation; do not assume a response scheduled much later still qualifies.

fields.alt: WhatFlow text-message action with recipient mapped from the incoming sender and a sample delivery reply
fields.caption: Inactive demo: Recipient Phone Number uses fromPhoneNumber. The 3–5 business day text is a sample policy, and replying TEAM does not itself assign a teammate.

children.text: What the demo actually does

In the demo store, the condition checks whether Message Body equals DELIVERY_INFO. The true branch sends the sample delivery-policy text to fromPhoneNumber. Sidekick generated those installed WhatFlow steps, and we inspected the recipient and message fields before saving the workflow inactive.

The sample answer mentions 3–5 business days and invites the buyer to reply TEAM. Replace that estimate with your real policy. TEAM is an invitation to continue the conversation, not a configured assignment action: the team still needs an inbox process or a separately supported routing workflow. No customer messages were sent during this demonstration.

fields.alt: Shopify Flow action picker listing WhatFlow WhatsApp message actions
fields.caption: WhatFlow message actions available in the demo store’s Shopify Flow editor. Message type and customer-service-window rules still apply.

children.text: Use button events for intent, and order replies for order work

A separate WhatsApp Button Clicked workflow can match the configured Button Text or Button Payload and choose the next response. Inspect the actual value from your setup rather than copying an imaginary universal identifier from a tutorial.

A button saying “My order” does not by itself identify an order. If the next step needs to tag a particular order, use a workflow with the required order context or ask a person to resolve the request. This distinction keeps an easy support menu from becoming an unreliable order automation.
Make the human handoff understandable

WhatFlow’s team inbox is where staff can read the conversation and respond when the rule is not enough. A message promising “I have assigned this to your account manager” would be misleading unless a supported action really performed that assignment. Use honest wording about the next step your team will actually follow.

If your store has an installed helpdesk connector with an appropriate action, Flow can use it to create a supported task or notification. Check that connector’s required customer identifiers and permissions. The generic text trigger does not automatically supply every field another app might need.
Set up
shared inbox ownership
before promising a team handoff.
Treat attachments as requests for review

WhatsApp media received is a separate trigger for images, videos, audio, documents and stickers. It can distinguish an attachment-based request from ordinary text. The supplied Meta media ID is not a public image URL; a temporary download URL, when supplied, expires and should stay private.

A photo is useful evidence for a colleague to review, not an automatic reason to approve a claim or refund. Keep customer attachments out of public spreadsheets, screenshots and documentation. Build a staff review path appropriate to the sensitivity of the request.
Test for silence as well as the expected reply

Try a matching keyword, a nonmatching message, a button tap and a repeated message with a controlled recipient. Confirm which branch runs, whether a response is attempted only once and whether the inbox conversation remains understandable. Also test the opt-out path: a STOP event should not start a promotional reply.

For a growing store, the economics of the handoff matter. WhatFlow Business API includes its features across plans and does not charge per inbox seat. You can involve another support colleague without a new seat subscription, while still budgeting for message allowances, rates and the other apps involved.
Use
Testing workflows in Shopify Flow
to distinguish inspecting a branch from executing an external reply.
Give the sample keyword an explicit no-reply case

Keep DELIVERY_INFO as the exact controlled condition in the inactive demonstration. Add a review note showing that an unrelated complaint should not receive the sample delivery-policy answer. Replace the sample delivery estimate with the store’s maintained policy before any later use, and name the inbox process that handles TEAM rather than implying an assignment action already exists.
Before you put this into practice
Inspect Message Body and sender-number mapping.
Check a matching keyword and a nonmatching complaint.
Review repeats, overlapping rules and STOP handling.
Assign ownership of TEAM replies and attachments.
Continue building your Shopify Flow setup

children.text: Use WhatFlow Business API’s WhatsApp Order Reply trigger when a customer’s response must update an identified Shopify order. Match the reply type and the configured button text or payload, then add a meaningful tag to the order supplied by that trigger. Keep nonmatching replies for review and test repeats and older messages without treating confirmation as automatic fulfillment authority.
Key takeaways
Use the order-specific trigger rather than a generic button event.
Match the actual configured answer before adding an order tag.
A confirmation tag does not itself authorize charging, refunding or fulfillment.
The useful outcome is the order decision

A customer tapping “Confirm order” is only half the job. The warehouse still needs to know what that answer means for the correct Shopify order. A practical workflow turns the response into an understandable store action, while giving staff a way to handle exceptions.

This recipe uses WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API and Shopify Flow. It is an order-reply workflow, not an instruction to fulfill, charge, cancel or refund an order automatically. The first outcome is deliberately modest: add a clear order tag after the intended confirmation response is matched.
Use WhatsApp Order Reply when the next action needs an order

Choose the WhatFlow trigger named WhatsApp Order Reply. Its extension supplies order and customer references together with Reply Type, Button Text, Button Payload and Message Body. Those references are the reason this trigger is appropriate for a Shopify order action.

Do not substitute the generic WhatsApp Button Clicked trigger merely because the buyer tapped a button. That event is useful for conversation routing, but its generic fields do not establish which Shopify order should be updated. If a workflow cannot identify the intended order, stop the order-changing branch and let a person investigate.
Shopify’s
Choosing the right Flow trigger
explains why the selected starting event determines the available workflow data.

fields.alt: Inactive Shopify Flow example branching on a WhatsApp order reply and adding an order tag
fields.caption: Inactive demo workflow: a WhatsApp order reply is checked before an order tag is added. The screenshot does not show a live order being changed or fulfilled.

children.text: Step 1: define the outbound message and its context

The customer needs a clear message about a particular order. When configuring a Flow message action from an order event, retain the provided order and customer context where available. Use an approved template when the outbound message requires one.

Decide exactly what the customer is being asked to confirm. Order confirmation, payment confirmation and permission to fulfill are different decisions. Keep the wording and the resulting tag consistent so the team does not interpret one answer as all three.
Review
outbound template configuration
when establishing the message’s supported order context.
Step 2: check the reply type and the chosen answer

In Flow, add a condition after WhatsApp Order Reply. For a button-based path, check that Reply Type is BUTTON and then match the actual Button Text or Button Payload used by the configured message. Use the value from your own message setup; do not assume every template uses CONFIRM as its internal identifier.

A typed reply follows a separate path. An exact short keyword can be a simple first rule, but a message containing negation or a question should not become an automatic positive confirmation just because it contains a familiar word.
Step 3: add an explicit Shopify order tag

On the matching branch, use Shopify’s supported order-tag action and choose a tag your team understands, such as WF_COD_CONFIRMED. Select the order supplied by the trigger. This is a visual field-selection task; it does not require writing an Admin API call.

Use a separate tag or staff process for requests that need review. A customer asking to change an address should not accidentally pass through the same positive branch as a straightforward confirmation.
Keep the nonmatching branch useful

A nonmatching answer can remain in the WhatFlow inbox for a person to handle. If your store has a suitable installed notification or helpdesk connector, you can add its supported action to the review branch. That requires the connector’s own setup and the relevant event data.

Do not add a cancellation, refund or fulfillment step simply to make the diagram look complete. Those actions have consequences beyond acknowledging a message, and the store should define their business rules separately.
Use
incoming message routing
for intent and support branches that do not identify an order.
Test the order association, not only the happy button

Use controlled recipients and test orders. Include a positive tap, a negative response, a typed question, a repeated tap and a reply to an older message. If the same buyer has more than one order, verify which record the trigger supplies before relying on the automation.

Check the resulting tag in Shopify and the conversation in WhatFlow. Repeated events should not create a new business decision or repeated customer replies simply because the buyer tapped twice. An order tag can be a useful guard in the workflow when you define the intended behavior for an already-handled order.
Why this is useful for a small operations team

The founder, support colleague and warehouse do not have to pass screenshots around to establish what happened. The reply starts a store workflow and the result is visible as part of the order process. WhatFlow’s included inbox remains the place for the human conversation when the answer is not straightforward.

WhatFlow Business API does not charge inbox seat fees or restrict its features to a higher plan. Messaging allowances and applicable delivery costs still apply. That makes it practical to give the people involved in fulfillment access to the same conversation without turning each handoff into another seat subscription.
Write expected results for the same buyer’s two orders

For a hypothetical review case, give one controlled buyer two test orders and an older confirmation message. Record which order each reply is expected to reference before inspecting the inactive workflow’s mapping. Add a repeated-tap case with the expected already-handled behavior. This checks the association and business rule rather than assuming that a familiar confirmation label identifies the newest order.
Before you put this into practice
Confirm WhatsApp Order Reply supplies the intended order reference.
Match the real reply type and configured button value.
Select the trigger’s order in the tagging action.
Review negative, typed, repeated and older-message replies.
Keep the demo inactive and consequential actions outside this tagging recipe.

children.text: Build a WhatsApp automation visually by selecting a Shopify or WhatFlow Business API trigger, adding a condition and choosing a supported action in Shopify Flow. Match the event’s data to the intended outcome and message rules. Start with an inactive, narrow workflow; inspect logic and field mapping before any separate controlled check of an actual external action.
Key takeaways
A trigger supplies context, a condition selects a branch and an action performs the task.
Choose order-aware events for order work and eligible formats for messages.
All WhatFlow Business API plans include features and no inbox seat fees; allowances and rates differ.
A customer reply can be the beginning of a workflow

A customer taps a button in WhatsApp. Instead of asking someone to copy that answer into Shopify, the store can let the response start a workflow: check what the buyer selected, add the appropriate order tag and bring a human into the conversation when the answer needs attention. That is the useful promise of WhatFlow’s Shopify Flow integration.

I’m Safwan Adnan, co-founder and CEO of WhatFlow. We built the integration so merchants can connect messaging with the rest of the store through Shopify’s own visual automation editor. For the standard workflows in this guide, you do not need to write an API request, maintain a webhook server or learn JSON. You choose the event, add the business condition and select an action.

These guides refer to WhatFlow WhatsApp Business API, our official Meta Cloud API app. The screenshots use a demo store and inactive example workflows. They illustrate configuration rather than measured revenue or delivery results.

Use Flow’s built-in test mode first to inspect the path and variable values. Shopify documents that this mode does not send notifications or change live store data, and external actions can show configuration previews instead of executing. A successful preview therefore checks logic and mapping; it is not proof of an actual WhatsApp send. Any end-to-end delivery check is a separate controlled exercise.
The three pieces: trigger, condition and action

A trigger starts the workflow when something happens. A condition asks a question about the event’s data. An action performs the selected task when the relevant branch is reached. Think of the process as a sentence: when this happens, if this is true, do that.

The visual editor lets you connect those steps and inspect each field. Shopify supplies store events and actions; installed apps can contribute their own. WhatFlow supplies events from WhatsApp and actions that send messages. That makes WhatsApp part of a wider store workflow rather than an isolated notification channel.
Shopify’s
Flow concepts and visual editor

children.text: Five incoming WhatFlow events to know

WhatsApp Text Message Received starts from an incoming text, product enquiry or supported ad-response context. It supplies fields such as Message Body and Sender Phone Number. A first useful recipe is to recognize a clear request and send a relevant reply.

WhatsApp Button Clicked starts from a quick-reply button tap. Its fields include the visible Button Text and the Button Payload. It is useful for intent routing, but a generic button event should not be treated as proof that the workflow has an identified Shopify order.

WhatsApp Order Reply is the order-specific option. It includes order and customer references as well as reply fields. Choose this when the next step needs to change an order tag or use order data, and test that the reply resolves to the intended order.

WhatsApp media received covers incoming images, videos, audio, documents and stickers. A store can distinguish an attachment from an ordinary text message and route it for attention. A received file is not automatically an approved claim, refund or proof of delivery.

WhatsApp Customer Opted Out represents an opt-out such as STOP that has been added to the WhatsApp blocklist. It is useful for coordinating other store processes around that preference. Do not turn the opt-out into a trigger for another promotional reply.
The lifecycle callback is not another customer event

The extension definitions also contain an internal lifecycle callback for Flow subscriptions. That supports the integration behind the scenes. It is not a sixth shopper-facing event to use as the start of a merchant workflow. The five triggers above are the useful incoming-message categories for the recipes in this series.
